record.tranche_reason: The post compares downstream benchmark performance of newer models with trends fitted to earlier models, testing predictability through benchmark scores rather than held-out pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The post uses Kaplan and Chinchilla scaling laws to estimate equivalent compute and position models on graphs; it does not independently test their loss laws or compute-optimal allocations. Comments cite other work but are not results of this post.
record.test_reason: The post fits sigmoids of normalized benchmark performance against estimated Chinchilla-equivalent compute (reducible loss) for GPT-3 and PaLM-1. It then checks whether PaLM-2 and GPT-4 land on those trends, a direct, informal test of V6. It uses the Kaplan and Chinchilla loss laws only as conversion tools and does not test V1–V5 or V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The author finds PaLM-2 and GPT-4 roughly on trend on average, with benchmark-specific over- and underperformance. He warns that the average weighting is arbitrary and the GPT-4 comparison is very noisy. He also suggests the PaLM-2 fit may be dominated by GPT-3 points, with PaLM-2 similar to PaLM. He notes GPT-4 might be slightly under-trend given algorithmic gains and fine-tuning.
record.recipe_differences: Uses downstream benchmark scores normalized between random and an estimated maximum, plotted against estimated Chinchilla-equivalent compute; fits sigmoid trends to earlier-model results and compares newer models. It does not directly measure held-out pretraining loss.
record.method_sensitivity: The estimated x-position changes with the chosen scaling-law conversion: the author reports the Kaplan- and Chinchilla-based graphs give different positions and trend slopes. PaLM-2's equivalent-compute estimate is uncertain; the author uses 7.3e24 FLOP for later fitting after considering bounds of 3.9e24 and 1.4e25 FLOP. Benchmark coverage and shot count differ between the PaLM-2 and GPT-4 comparisons.

fits_no_version.finding: Switching the x-axis from Kaplan-based to Chinchilla-based compute compresses the points and steepens the slope. This moves the extrapolated 90% average point from ~1e28 to ~5e26 FLOP.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream-performance extrapolations in compute depend strongly on which loss scaling law is used to place models on the compute axis.

record.problems: The post supplies qualitative trend comparisons without benchmark-score values or statistical uncertainty. Benchmark weighting is acknowledged to be arbitrary. PaLM-2's compute estimate relies on a leak and assumptions about model type and training; the PaLM-2 graph uses 1-shot results while earlier posts focused on few-shot results. GPT-4 has only four reported benchmarks here, making its extrapolation noisy.
record.rows_left_out: No text-described result bearing on V6 was left out. Individual plotted values not described in the text are not extracted.

untested.parts: Quantitative prediction error; uncertainty on the fits; any models beyond PaLM-2 and GPT-4; predictions from directly measured pretraining loss (x-positions are estimated, not measured).
Not tested: Chinchilla/Kaplan loss laws used only as conversion tools.
Not tested; Chinchilla 20 tokens/param ratio assumed.
Not tested for loss exponents; the author only notes that Kaplan vs Chinchilla conversion changes x-positions.

record.verdict_notes: This is an informal Alignment Forum post: qualitative judgments read off graphs, with no numbers or uncertainty. The x-positions are estimates (leaked PaLM-2 parameter and token counts; Epoch's GPT-4 compute), so the 'on trend' verdicts are only as good as those estimates. The comments (BNSL, multimodality) are not results of this study.

versions.untested_parts: No independent measurement of held-out pretraining loss against parameters, tokens, or compute.
No extrapolation test of held-out pretraining loss from small runs to much larger runs.
No measurement of loss-minimising parameter and token allocations across compute budgets.
No comparison of architectures at fixed parameter count.
No testing of power-law scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
Tests benchmark-performance trends for selected categories, not broad downstream task coverage or prediction from measured pretraining loss.
Does not independently test how fitted loss exponents or compute-optimal splits vary with setup, or whether loss curves bend away from power laws.

rows.operation_detail: Plots benchmark performance against estimated Chinchilla-equivalent compute and fits an average sigmoid.

conditions.value: the post's benchmark set; equal weight assigned to each benchmark

rows.measure: normalized benchmark performance; compute at which the fitted average sigmoid reaches 90%
rows.baseline: Prior graph using a Kaplan-law x-axis: ~1e28 FLOP for 90%
rows.note: The author says the new graph's average sigmoid reaches 90% at about this compute; benchmark weighting is described as arbitrary.
rows.check: Not an outcome test. It reports how the extrapolated 90% point moves (~1e28 to ~5e26 FLOP) when the x-axis changes from Kaplan-based to Chinchilla-based, with no new data. It is a projection that depends on an axis choice, so it says nothing on whether downstream performance tracks scale. It is better recorded under fits_no_version.
